introduction: Bartók Béla út grew from a Buda road that carried two different names before the First World War and was renamed twice more. Rail and tram lines reached it in the 1890s, long before the cafés and galleries of today.
chapters: Fehérvári út and Átlós út, 1874 to 1920

According to the Hungarian Wikipedia article on the street, the section from Szent Gellért tér to Móricz Zsigmond körtér was called Fehérvári út from 1874 to 1920. The section from the körtér to Vasút utca, near Kelenföld railway station, was called Átlós út, but only from 1890 to 1920. Both names describe a road leading out of Buda towards the south and west rather than a boulevard of the kind it became. Building along the route followed the zoning plan of 1913, which set the pattern of the residential blocks of three to five storeys that line most of it today.
Rails and trams reach the road, 1898 to 1942

Transport arrived early. A tram ran along the street for the first time in 1898, linking Kelenföld railway station with Móricz Zsigmond körtér. In 1899 the Dél-Budai HÉV suburban railway started from Szent Gellért tér along Fehérvári út, splitting after Albertfalva into one branch for Budaörs and Törökbálint and another for Budafok and Nagytétény. Trams 19 and 49 began service in 1910, and the Kelenföld tram depot has operated since 1912. In 1942 the HÉV was shortened to the building known as the Gomba at the körtér, which was completed that year.
New names and recent renewal, 1920 to today

In 1920 the Council of Public Works renamed Fehérvári út and its continuation, Átlós út, as Horthy Miklós út. In 1945 the road was renamed Bartók Béla út. The cobblestones were replaced with asphalt in 2002 and 2003, the reconstruction reached Kelenföld railway station in 2005, and the tram track between Szent Gellért tér and Móricz Zsigmond körtér was renovated in 2016. After the M4 metro opened and bus traffic fell, the Bartók-negyed programme strengthened the cultural role of the stretch between the körtér and Szent Gellért tér, the same stretch that now holds many of the street's cafés and galleries.

stories.title: The composer's will and the street's name
description: The Hungarian Wikipedia article suggests that the choice of Bartók's name in 1945 may have been symbolic. It notes that the composer opposed Nazi-aligned ideas and left Hungary after the First World War, and that in his 1940 will he stated that his name should not be used for public spaces in Hungary while places in Budapest were named after Hitler and Mussolini.

introduction: The Várkert Bazár was planned in the early 1870s and built between 1875 and 1883 to designs by Miklós Ybl. It then passed through studios, schools and a rock-concert venue, was closed in 1984, and was restored in 2014.
chapters: Ybl's complex below the palace, 1875 to 1883

The building's own history page says the idea of a representative building complex and ornamental garden at the foot of Castle Hill arose in the early 1870s, and that Miklós Ybl was given the task of drawing the final plans. The neo-Renaissance complex was built between 1875 and 1883. A history of Buda Castle describes an open arcade with pavilions, stairways, ramps and two blocks of flats. The arcades were meant for shops and workshops, and the gardens were laid out to keep an open view of the Danube from the Royal Palace. Ybl died in 1891, before the palace reconstruction he had planned was finished.
Studios, schools and a Youth Park, 1884 to 1984

According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the north wing housed a craftswomen's training workshop from 1883 to 1888, the Historical Portrait Gallery from 1890 to 1895 and a women's painting school from about 1890 until 1918. From 1884 the sculptor Alajos Stróbl had a studio in the arcade, the first of about eighty artists who worked there over the next century. The building was heavily damaged in the Second World War. From 1961 it became the Budai Ifjúsági Park, a venue for pop and rock concerts. A staircase wall collapsed during an Edda concert in 1980, and the Youth Park ended in 1984, when the building was closed.
Closure and restoration, 1984 to 2014

After 1984 the building decayed, and a Visit Hungary article says it was listed among the hundred most endangered monuments in the world. Several plans for its reconstruction and reuse were drawn up before Government Decree 1375 of 2011 launched the reconstruction, with work beginning in summer 2013. Excavations found medieval and Ottoman-era objects, remains of cannon foundries of the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries and cannonballs likely from 1686. The Triton fountain was restored. The first phase reopened on 3 April 2014, and a second phase, with an event centre, an underground garage and a Renaissance garden, followed on 29 August 2014.

stories.title: Franz Joseph and the view he rarely saw
description: Visit Hungary records a story told about the gardens: according to legend, Emperor Franz Joseph rarely enjoyed the Danube view that the Neo-Renaissance gardens were designed to keep open, because he never stayed overnight in the Castle. The article presents this as a legend, not as a documented fact.

introduction: The Matthias Fountain was made by Alajos Stróbl between 1899 and 1904 as part of the great reconstruction of the Buda palace. It lost a figure in the Second World War and was restored in 2010.
chapters: The palace that needed a fountain, 1875 to 1912

English Wikipedia's history of Buda Castle says the rebuilding of the palace spanned 1875 to 1912. Miklós Ybl drew a master plan in 1885 and work began in 1890, and after his death in 1891 Alajos Hauszmann took over. Hauszmann designed the north wing, which doubled the Baroque palace on the Danube side. The same history places Alajos Stróbl's fountain in the western forecourt near the rear facade of that wing, as part of Hauszmann's work. The fountain's own article credits Hauszmann as master builder of the palace reconstruction and as the man who erected the fountain.
Stróbl's hunting group, 1899 to 1904

According to English Wikipedia, King Franz Joseph approved the scheme, and Stróbl began work in 1899. He modelled the stag on a large animal killed by poachers in 1896 in a forest where he had gone hunting, and Duke Pálffy sent him the hounds that served as models. The figure of the henchman won a state gold medal in 1901. The fountain was inaugurated in 1904 in the presence of the king. It shows King Matthias Corvinus in hunting dress above a dead stag, with Szép Ilonka and the chronicler Galeotto Marzio at the sides of the basin.
War damage and restoration, 1944 to 2010

The group suffered in the Second World War, when the middle dog sculpture was destroyed. The sculptor Jenő Grantner reconstructed it. Wikipedia adds that the original balustrade and mansard roof, which had been more elaborate, were simplified after the war damage. This matches the wider history of the palace, which was reduced to ruins in the siege of 1944 and 1945 and rebuilt in the following decades. The fountain was restored in 2010, and it stands today in the palace forecourt that Visit Buda Castle calls the Hunyadi Courtyard.

stories.title: Szép Ilonka and the king
description: One of the figures at the basin is Szép Ilonka, Helen the Fair, shown protecting her tame fawn. She is the heroine of a nineteenth-century ballad by Mihály Vörösmarty. According to the ballad, Ilonka and Matthias fell in love when he was hunting without revealing who he was; when she learned his true identity she assumed the love was impossible and died of a broken heart. This is a literary legend, not a documented event.

introduction: The terrace takes its name from Prince Eugene of Savoy, whose equestrian statue by József Róna was placed before the Buda palace in 1900. The statue was first made for the town of Zenta and was bought for the palace instead.
chapters: Prince Eugene and Buda

Prince Eugene of Savoy was born in Paris on 18 October 1663 and died in Vienna on 21 April 1736. According to Hungary Today, he served as deputy commander of the Christian forces that liberated Buda in 1686. On 11 September 1697 he defeated a numerically superior Ottoman army at the Battle of Zenta, a victory the same article credits with ending roughly 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary. He also owned the island of Csepel, where he built a castle at Ráckeve, and Promontor, today's Budafok, was part of his estate.
A statue meant for Zenta, 1900

The equestrian statue is the work of József Róna. One account says the city of Zenta ordered it to commemorate the victory of 1697 but could not pay for the bronze, which waited in the sculptor's studio and then in front of the Art Gallery's main entrance. Prime Minister Kálmán Széll suggested that Emperor Franz Joseph buy it, and he did so on the basis of photographs. The statue was installed in 1900 in front of the main facade of the Royal Palace in Buda. A list of equestrian statues in Hungary also gives it as by József Róna, in the Buda Castle, 1900.
Siege, ruin and return, 1944 to the 1950s

The palace around the statue changed greatly after the siege of Budapest. English Wikipedia says that fighting between 29 December 1944 and 13 February 1945 reduced the palace to ruins. The Baroque horseshoe staircase behind the statue was demolished in the 1950s and not restored. The statue itself came through the siege relatively intact and, after restoration, returned to its original place. Today the terrace in front of the Hungarian National Gallery, with the statue at its centre, looks out over the Danube towards the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the city's bridges.

introduction: Trinity Square in the Buda Castle District took its open form only after the Ottoman occupation ended in 1686. Its Holy Trinity Column was inaugurated on 11 June 1713 as a thanks-offering after the plague.
chapters: Houses before 1686 and the open square after

The Buda Castle District heritage site stresses that this is not an old square. Until the end of the Ottoman occupation in 1686 a block of houses stood on the site. Before then, the Town Hall and the Nagyboldogasszony parish church, today's Matthias Church, were linked only by a narrow lane, and a row of houses stood directly in front of the church. When these houses were demolished, the church frontage became visible and the space between church and Town Hall was opened up. In the eighteenth century the parish church was run by the Jesuits, with a monastery on the north side and a three-storey seminary on the south, and a Baroque Town Hall stood at the corner of Tárnok and Szentháromság streets.
The plague columns, 1694 to 1713

The Council of Buda decided in 1694 to erect a Holy Trinity Column to protect the town from recurring plague, in gratitude for the end of an epidemic. The foundation stone was laid in 1700, and the first statue was finished in 1706 by the architect Ceresola Vereio and the stone carver Bernát Ferretti. In 1709, during another epidemic, it was removed to the Újlak suburb, and the magistrate ordered a larger and more decorative replacement. The present column was erected between 1710 and 1713 and inaugurated on 11 June 1713, made by Fülöp Ungleich with reliefs and coats of arms by Antal Hörger. A spring-fed well with a statue of Pallas Athene was completed on the square in 1718.
Rebuilding and ruin, 1890s to 1945

Around the end of the nineteenth century the parish church was converted into a coronation church. The northern side of the church was cleared, the former seminary to the south was demolished, and the south-eastern side of the square opened towards the Fisherman's Bastion. On the north side the former buildings were cleared and the former Ministry of Finance was built. The heritage site shows photographs of the Jesuit convent being demolished around 1900 and of Matthias Church in ruins in 1945. It says the square's present form differs greatly from its Baroque layout because of town replanning and reconstruction after the Second World War.
